My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds to an integer polynomial  

\[
a(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x]
\]

with degree ≤ 8, and the defining condition is equivalent to the existence of integers k≠l and a polynomial b(x)∈ℤ[x] such that  

\[
a(x)\,b(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{\min(k,l)}\bigl(1+x^{|k-l|}\bigr).
\]

Thus α is shifty **iff** its polynomial a(x) divides a binomial \(x^{m}+x^{n}\) (with m≠n) in ℤ[x]. This reduces the counting problem to enumerating all integer‑coefficient divisors of some binomial whose non‑zero terms lie in degrees 0…8.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to an integer polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}
\]

with degree ≤ 8 such that there exist integers \(k\neq l\) and an integer polynomial \(B(x)\) satisfying  

\[
A(x)B(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{\min(k,l)}\bigl(1+x^{|k-l|}\bigr).
\]

Hence \(A(x)\) must be a divisor (in \(\mathbb Z[x]\)) of a monomial times a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) (\(d=|k-l|>0\)).  Equivalently, every shifty α is of the form  

\[
A(x)=x^{e}\,D(x),\qquad e\ge0,\;D(x)\mid(1+x^{d})\text{ in }\mathbb Z[x],
\]

with the additional constraint \(e+\deg D\le8\).  This reduction to divisors of \(1+x^{d}\) is the key step toward counting the shifty functions.

My current finding is that the condition “∃ β, k≠l such that Sₙ(α)⋆β = 1 iff n∈{k,l}” is equivalent to the existence of a Laurent‑polynomial G(x) with integer coefficients and a polynomial A(x)=∑_{i=0}^{8}α(i)x^{i} (degree ≤ 8, no negative powers) such that  

\[
A(x)\,G(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{\min(k,l)}\bigl(1+x^{|k-l|}\bigr).
\]

Thus a “shifty’’ α is exactly a polynomial of degree ≤ 8 that divides a binomial \(x^{p}+x^{q}\) (with p≠q) in the ring ℤ[x,x^{-1}].  In particular, after factoring out the smallest exponent, the only non‑trivial factor to consider is \(1+x^{d}\) with d=|k‑l|>0.  Hence α must be a divisor (in ℤ[x]) of some polynomial of the form \(1+x^{d}\) where d is a positive integer.  This reduction turns the original functional problem into a purely algebraic divisor‑counting problem.

My current finding is that the condition “∃ β, k≠ℓ such that  Sₙ(α)⋆β = 1 for n∈{k,ℓ} and 0 otherwise” is equivalent to the existence of integers p,r,s and a polynomial C(x)∈ℤ[x] with C(0)≠0 such that  

\[
A(x)\,C(x)=x^{r}+x^{s},
\]

where \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\) is the generating polynomial of α. In other words, α is shifty iff its polynomial A(x) (degree ≤ 8) divides a binomial sum of two monomials in ℤ[x] (up to a power of x). This reduces the problem to counting the 9‑coefficient integer vectors whose polynomial divisor property holds.

My current finding is that a shifty function \(\alpha\) (with support in \(\{0,\dots ,8\}\)) is exactly a polynomial  

\[
a(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}
\]

that can be written as  

\[
a(x)=x^{s}\,p(x)
\]

where \(s\ge 0\) and \(p(x)\) is an integer‑coefficient divisor of a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) for some integer \(d>0\).  Equivalently, \(p(x)\) is a product (up to a sign) of any subset of the cyclotomic factors \(\Phi_{n}(x)\) that appear in the factorisation  

\[
x^{d}+1=\prod_{\substack{n\mid 2d\\ n\nmid d}}\Phi_{n}(x).
\]

Thus \(\alpha\) is shifty iff its generating polynomial is a monomial \(x^{s}\) times a divisor of some \(1+x^{d}\) and has degree \(\le 8\). This reduces the counting problem to enumerating all such products with \(\deg(x^{s}p)\le8\).

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a non‑zero primitive integer polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}
\]

that divides a binomial \(x^{d}+1\) for some integer \(d>0\).  Indeed, writing the correlation condition as  

\[
\sum_{t=0}^{8}\alpha(t)\beta(t-n)=\begin{cases}1&n\in\{k,l\}\\0&\text{else}\end{cases}
\]

and using generating functions gives \(A(x)B(x^{-1})=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{\min(k,l)}(1+x^{|k-l|})\).  Cancelling the monomial factor shows that \(A(x)\) must divide \(1+x^{d}\) (with \(d=|k-l|>0\)).  Consequently, counting shifty functions reduces to counting primitive integer polynomials of degree ≤ 8 that are divisors of some \(x^{d}+1\).

\[

\]

where \(d(x)\) is an integer‑coefficient divisor of a binomial \(1+x^{s}\) for some \(s\ge1\).  Indeed, the condition \(S_{n}(\alpha)\star\beta=1_{\{k,l\}}\) is equivalent to a factorisation  

\[
A(x)\,G(x)=x^{m}(1+x^{s})
\]

in the Laurent polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\); the monomial \(x^{m}\) can be absorbed into \(G\), leaving \(A(x)=x^{t}d(x)\) with \(d(x)\mid(1+x^{s})\) and \(\deg A\le8\).  Thus every shifty \(\alpha\) corresponds exactly to a pair \((t,d)\) satisfying these constraints.

\[

\]

with \(0\le t\le8\) and where \(d(x)\) is an integer‑coefficient divisor of a binomial \(1+x^{s}\) for some \(s\ge1\) (i.e. \(d(x)\mid 1+x^{s}\) in ℤ[x]).  The shift \(t\) guarantees that all exponents of A lie in \([0,8]\).  Conversely, any such \(A(x)\) yields a β (take the complementary factor \(x^{m} (1+x^{s})/d(x)\) with a suitable monomial shift) so that \(S_n(α)\starβ\) equals 1 exactly at two distinct n.  Hence the counting problem reduces to enumerating all integer‑polynomial divisors of binomials \(1+x^{s}\) whose degree ≤8 after a monomial shift.

My current finding is that **Solver 3’s extra condition is false**: a shifty function does **not** require all cyclotomic factors to have the same 2‑adic valuation.  

Indeed, any α with generating polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\pm x^{s}\prod_{i}\Phi_{2m_i}(x)
\]

(where each \(m_i\) divides some integer \(d\)) satisfies the definition, because  

\[
A(x)\,C(x)=x^{s}\Bigl(\prod_i\Phi_{2m_i}(x)\Bigr)C(x)=x^{k}+x^{\ell}
\]

with \(C(x)=x^{k-s}+x^{\ell-s}\).  
For example, \(A(x)=\Phi_{2}(x)\Phi_{12}(x)= (x+1)(x^{4}-x^{2}+1)=x^{5}+x^{4}+x^{3}+x^{2}+x+1\) (degree 5) works, yet its factors have 2‑adic valuations 1 and 2, contradicting Solver 3’s “same 2‑adic valuation’’ claim. Thus the correct classification is the one given by Solver 2: a shifty α is exactly a monomial times a divisor (up to sign) of some binomial \(1+x^{d}\).

\]

where the inner sum runs over all subsets of cyclotomic polynomials with the same 2‑adic valuation and total degree ≤ 8.  This yields **160** shifty functions.
